=== Pro Se Intervenor Mark Allan Bradbury's Reply to Exceptions.docx ===
PUC DOCKET NO. 59475
SOAH DOCKET NO. 473-26-16349
PRO SE INTERVENOR MARK ALLAN BRADBURY'S REPLY TO EXCEPTIONS TO THE PROPOSAL FOR DECISION
TO THE HONORABLE COMMISSIONERS OF THE PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION OF TEXAS:
Pro Se Intervenor Mark Allan Bradbury ("Bradbury") timely files this Reply to Exceptions to the Proposal for Decision ("PFD"). Bradbury respectfully requests that the Commission adopt the PFD's primary recommendation and deny the applications. Alternatively, if the Commission rejects denial and approves the Bell County East-to-Big Hill Project, the Commission should reject the PFD's contingent selection of Route 894 and select Route 487 as the route that best satisfies PURA § 37.056 and 16 TAC § 25.101.
I. SUMMARY OF POSITION
The exceptions present three analytically distinct issues: need, notice, and routing. They should remain distinct. Applicants seek reversal of the PFD on need and notice. Applicants' Exceptions, PUC Interchange Item No. 6484, pp. 6-78. Delaware Basin Midstream LLC ("DBM") likewise seeks reversal on need. DBM Exceptions, Item No. 6481, pp. 4-11. Commission Staff also disagrees with the PFD on need and notice, but Staff separately and expressly excepts to the PFD's selection of Route 894 and recommends Route 487. Commission Staff's Exceptions, Item No. 6471, pp. 3, 13-21.
Accordingly, even if the Commission disagrees with the PFD on need or notice, it should not automatically adopt Route 894. The routing record must still be independently weighed. On that question, Staff concludes that Route 487 best meets the statutory and regulatory criteria. Item 6471, p. 3. The J27/J25/J4 Opposition Landowners independently reach the same conclusion if a Central Corridor route is selected. Item No. 6465, pp. 2, 7-11.
II. APPLICANTS' AND DBM'S NEED EXCEPTIONS SHOULD BE OVERRULED
A. The PBRP recommendation does not replace the CCN burden of proof.
Applicants devote the principal portion of their exceptions to load forecasts, Far West Texas import constraints, the Bell County East injection point, the 2030 timeline, the weight to be given ERCOT, generation alternatives, and project alternatives. Item 6484, pp. 10-40. DBM similarly argues that the PFD conflicts with findings in Docket Nos. 59029 and 59315 and improperly requires a project-specific or partial-build study. Item 6481, pp. 5-11.
Those arguments do not eliminate the threshold requirement in PURA § 37.056(a): the certificate before the Commission must be shown necessary for the service, accommodation, convenience, or safety of the public. The Commission's approval of the Permian Basin Reliability Plan is important planning evidence, but the CCN proceeding remains the forum in which the statutory showing must be made on the evidentiary record for this project. The PFD was therefore entitled to test the assumptions supporting the recommendation against later and contrary evidence developed at hearing.
B. Changed load evidence is material, not collateral.
Applicants characterize post-PBRP load developments as insufficient to disturb ERCOT's recommendation. Item 6484, pp. 13-20. Staff also relies on the fact that ERCOT has not withdrawn its recommendation. Item 6471, pp. 9-13. But the relevant question is not simply whether the recommendation remains formally outstanding. The question is whether the record still supports the magnitude, configuration, timing, and public necessity of the facilities requested in this CCN. The PFD's consideration of changed circumstances therefore goes directly to the statutory need inquiry.
C. Later Far West planning does not automatically prove the specific Import Path 2 configuration.
Applicants and Staff cite ERCOT's later planning concerning the North-to-Far-West and South-to-Far-West Generic Transmission Constraints. Item 6484, pp. 20-27; Item 6471, pp. 10-13. That evidence may support a need for additional transmission capability, but it does not logically establish that every component and capacity assumption of the proposed Import Path 2 must be approved exactly as filed. The Commission may consider later planning without treating it as a substitute for the project-specific statutory showing.
D. Considering generation alternatives is not the same as ordering generation.
Applicants argue that the PFD improperly relied on generation alternatives in a competitive market. Item 6484, pp. 35-39. The distinction is straightforward: no party need ask the Commission to compel construction of generation in order to ask whether local or nearer generation was adequately evaluated as a planning alternative before committing ratepayers and landowners to a massive long-distance 765-kV buildout. Alternative analysis informs whether the proposed transmission facilities are necessary; it does not convert the Commission into a generation planner.
E. Companion-docket findings are relevant but not dispositive.
DBM relies heavily on need findings in Docket Nos. 59029 and 59315. Item 6481, pp. 5-8. Those decisions are relevant context, but this docket contains its own application, evidentiary record, PFD, and route-specific consequences. The Commission should decide the statutory need question on this record rather than treating a companion proceeding as preclusive.
III. APPLICANTS' NOTICE EXCEPTIONS DO NOT ERASE THE ROUTE-DEVELOPMENT RECORD
Applicants challenge both the PFD's public-meeting analysis and its interpretation of "current county tax rolls," and they contend denial is not an available remedy. Item 6484, pp. 41-76. Staff similarly excepts to the notice findings. Item 6471, pp. 4-9. Bradbury preserves the PFD's notice conclusions.
At minimum, however, the underlying facts remain relevant to routing and community values even if the Commission adopts a narrower legal interpretation of Rule 22.52. The exceptions of the J27/J25/J4 Opposition Landowners recognize that the Commission's August 28, 2026 order in Docket No. 59315 rejected the PFD's Rule 22.52(a)(4) interpretation, while preserving the factual history of route expansion and community participation. Item 6465, pp. 1-3. Thus, a legal ruling that notice was sufficient does not turn the absence of comparable pre-application participation on later-developed links into evidence favoring Route 894.
IV. IF THE PROJECT IS APPROVED, THE COMMISSION SHOULD SELECT ROUTE 487
A. Commission Staff affirmatively recommends Route 487.
Staff states that Route 487 best meets PURA § 37.056 and 16 TAC § 25.101. Item 6471, p. 3. Staff then devotes its routing exceptions to explaining why the PFD improperly discounted qualitative and quantitative criteria in which Route 487 outperforms Route 894 and the other focus routes. Id. at pp. 13-21. This is not merely an objection to Route 894; it is an affirmative recommendation by the Commission's technical Staff after review of the record.
B. Route 487 is the shortest and least expensive of Staff's four focus routes.
Staff identifies Route 487 at 221.50 miles, compared with 223.17 miles for Route 894, 223.78 miles for Route 296, and 229.02 miles for Route 392. Item 6471, pp. 18-19. Staff also identifies Route 487's estimated transmission-line cost at approximately $1.665 billion and explains that it is about $16 million cheaper than Route 894 and between $16 million and $50 million cheaper than the other focus routes. Id. at pp. 17-19. Those differences are not immaterial merely because the project is exceptionally large.
C. Route 487 has the strongest compatible-corridor performance among the focus routes.
Staff describes paralleling as perhaps the most compelling reason to prefer Route 487. Route 487 parallels or utilizes compatible right-of-way for about 50% of its length, approximately 110 miles, including about 22.1 miles of existing transmission-line right-of-way. Item 6471, pp. 19-20. The J27/J25/J4 Opposition Landowners provide the more precise comparison: Route 487 has approximately 109.95 miles (49.64%) of compatible-ROW paralleling versus approximately 98.02 miles (43.92%) for Route 894, and approximately 22.05 miles of existing-transmission-line paralleling versus 5.66 miles for Route 894. Item 6465, p. 8.
That distinction matters on a 200-foot-wide 765-kV corridor. Greater use of existing compatible corridors consolidates infrastructure and reduces the amount of new standalone corridor imposed on previously unencumbered property.
D. Route 487 has fewer mapped stream crossings and other environmental advantages.
Staff identifies 282 mapped stream crossings for Route 487, fewer than Route 894 and every other focus route. Item 6471, pp. 16-17. The J27/J25/J4 Opposition Landowners quantify the comparison as 282 for Route 487 versus 291 for Route 894 and also identify less mileage of known federally listed species habitat and less mileage of high archaeological/historical-site potential on Route 487. Item 6465, p. 9. These metrics reinforce Staff's conclusion that the PFD gave insufficient weight to Route 487's overall environmental performance.
E. Park proximity should be weighed, but it should not control the entire route selection.
The strongest argument against Route 487 is its proximity to Colorado Bend and Post Oak Ridge State Parks. Staten Creek Ranch and 4K Land emphasize those qualitative impacts and urge a Northern Corridor route. Items 6477 and 6478. Staff nevertheless concludes that the park factor does not outweigh Route 487's cumulative advantages. Item 6471, pp. 13-21. Route 894 is not impact-free: it too affects the park/recreational landscape. The Commission should therefore compare incremental park impacts against the full set of statutory factors rather than allow a single criterion to override cost, length, paralleling, stream crossings, prudent avoidance, and landowner impacts.
F. Route 894's habitable-structure advantage is limited.
The focus-route data cited by Staff show 85 habitable structures within 500 feet of Route 894 and 96 for Route 487. Item 6471, pp. 18-20. The J27/J25/J4 Opposition Landowners note that the single-family-residence comparison is 80 versus 85, a difference of five. Item 6465, p. 9. Prudent avoidance deserves weight, but the Commission has never reduced route selection to a single structure-count metric. Here, the modest structure advantage for Route 894 must be weighed against Route 487's stronger corridor utilization, lower cost, shorter length, and environmental metrics.
V. ROUTE 296 DOES NOT DISPLACE ROUTE 487
A substantial group of intervenors advocates Route 296 or a modified Route 296. See Items 6453, 6454, 6455, 6456, 6463, 6473, 6476, 6485, and 6486. Their criticisms of Route 894 are significant and should be credited where supported by the record. But the existence of a strong anti-894 case does not establish Route 296 as superior to Route 487.
Staff's focus-route analysis favors Route 487: it is shorter than Route 296, uses more compatible right-of-way, has fewer mapped stream crossings, and has fewer habitable structures on the data Staff cites. Item 6471, pp. 16, 18-20. The PFD also identified the proximity of Route 296 to Florence Elementary School and two churches as a material disadvantage. Id. at pp. 15-16. The Commission should not replace the Staff-recommended filed route with a modified or hybrid route unless the record establishes that the modification itself has been adequately evaluated under the same criteria.
VI. ROUTES 392 AND 410 DO NOT PROVIDE A BETTER OVERALL BALANCE THAN ROUTE 487
Staten Creek Ranch urges Route 392 or Route 410, emphasizing their Northern Corridor crossing and avoidance of the Central Corridor's state-park impacts. Item 6477, pp. 1-5, 26-34. 4K Land likewise argues that Northern Corridor routes perform better under its weighted suitability analysis. Item 6478, pp. 7-10. Those arguments identify genuine qualitative considerations, but they do not overcome Route 487's overall statutory balance.
For Route 392, Staff identifies 229.02 miles of length, 324 mapped stream crossings, and 136 habitable structures, compared with Route 487's 221.50 miles, 282 stream crossings, and 96 habitable structures. Item 6471, pp. 16, 18-20. Staff also notes that Route 392 uses about 23.6 miles of existing transmission-line right-of-way but parallels compatible right-of-way for only about 88.5 miles of its 229.02-mile length (38.6%), well below Route 487's approximately 50%. Id. at pp. 19-21.
Route 410 improves on Route 392 in some respects, but Staten Creek Ranch itself identifies Route 410 as approximately 10.47 miles longer than Route 894, approximately $56.5 million more expensive than Route 894, and within 500 feet of 98 habitable structures. Item 6477, pp. 30-34. Route 410 was not Staff's selected route after its record review. The Northern Corridor's park advantage therefore must be weighed against materially greater length, cost, and new-corridor burden.
VII. ROUTE 891 DOES NOT DISPLACE THE FULLY DEVELOPED STAFF RECOMMENDATION FOR ROUTE 487
Jerome and Gaylynn Sneed urge Route 891, emphasizing property-boundary paralleling, fewer miles of landowner-property bisection, an estimated cost nearly $9 million below Route 894, watershed protection, habitable structures, and the Pecan Valley Airport. Item 6483, pp. 9-22. Those are substantial arguments and the Commission should address them.
But Route 891 was not developed in the PFD's focus-route analysis to the same degree as Route 487, and Staff did not replace its recommendation of Route 487. The Sneeds' own filing acknowledges that the PFD gave Route 891 only limited discussion. Item 6483, pp. 9-11. Where Route 487 was fully litigated, compared, and affirmatively recommended by Staff, a late-emerging alternative should displace it only upon a clear record showing of overall superiority. The exceptions do not establish that showing.
VIII. THE EXCEPTIONS SUPPORTING ROUTE 894 DO NOT OVERCOME STAFF'S COMPARATIVE ANALYSIS
The Moseley Group/V8 Landowners Coalition, Brady Creek intervenors, CE Stephens Properties, and Theon Ranches or related parties defend Route 894 if the Project is approved. See Items 6457, 6468, 6469, and 6470. Their arguments include the J22 Colorado River crossing, park-distance considerations, prudent avoidance, and the PFD's view that Route 894 presents the best overall compromise.
Those points should be weighed, but Staff's contrary conclusion is better supported by the cumulative quantitative record: Route 487 is shorter, cheaper, has substantially more compatible-ROW use, parallels far more existing transmission-line right-of-way, and has fewer mapped stream crossings. Item 6471, pp. 16-21. The Commission should not allow one localized advantage to overwhelm that broader balance.
IX. CULTURAL-RESOURCE AND PUBLIC-SAFETY EXCEPTIONS SUPPORT APPROPRIATE CONDITIONS IF THE PROJECT IS APPROVED
The Comanche Nation seeks tribal monitoring and enhanced cultural-resource best management practices if a route is approved. Item 6462, pp. 8-11, 23-26. Burnet County seeks protections addressing emergency/public-safety communications. Item 6472. Those issues reinforce the need for careful mitigation and ordering provisions if the Commission authorizes construction. They do not supply a reason to prefer Route 894 over Route 487.
X. REQUESTED REVISIONS TO THE PFD IF THE COMMISSION APPROVES THE PROJECT
If the Commission rejects the PFD's primary recommendation to deny the applications, Bradbury respectfully requests that the Commission revise the PFD's contingent routing determination to reflect the following record-supported propositions:
Route 487 best meets the applicable routing criteria among the focus routes when the factors in PURA § 37.056 and 16 TAC § 25.101 are considered together.
Route 487 is approximately 221.50 miles long and is the shortest of Staff's four focus routes.
Route 487 has an estimated transmission-line cost of approximately $1.665 billion and is approximately $16 million less expensive than Route 894.
Route 487 parallels or utilizes compatible right-of-way for approximately 50% of its length (about 110 miles), including approximately 22.1 miles of existing transmission-line right-of-way.
Route 487 has approximately 282 mapped stream crossings, fewer than the other focus routes identified by Staff.
Although Route 894 has fewer habitable structures within 500 feet and a relative park-proximity advantage, those advantages do not outweigh Route 487's cumulative benefits in length, cost, corridor utilization, existing transmission-line paralleling, and environmental metrics.
If the Project is approved, Route 487 should replace Route 894 as the Commission-approved route.
XI. PRAYER
WHEREFORE, PREMISES CONSIDERED, Mark Allan Bradbury respectfully requests that the Commission overrule the exceptions seeking reversal of the PFD's primary denial recommendation and deny the applications. Alternatively, if the Commission approves the Bell County East-to-Big Hill Project, Bradbury requests that the Commission reject Route 894, adopt Commission Staff's recommendation of Route 487, revise the PFD's findings, conclusions, and ordering provisions accordingly, impose appropriate cultural-resource and public-safety mitigation supported by the record, and grant such other relief to which Bradbury may be entitled.

Respectfully submitted,

/s/ Mark Allan Bradbury
Mark Allan Bradbury
504 Grand Ave, Brady Texas 76825
